newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Spain's April budget deficit boosts EMU bid.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Spain's April budget deficit boosts EMU bid.

text.p: Spain's public deficit narrowed dramatically in the four months to April, enhancing the country's chances of meeting the budget target to qualify for a single European currency.
The deficit fell to 0.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) on a national account basis in the first four months of the year versus 1.1 percent in the first quarter.
"The thing to focus on is the deficit on a national account basis and this figure is looking very encouraging," said Gwyn Hacche, economist at HSBC in London.

In absolute terms, the state deficit on a national account basis, the measure relevant to the Maastricht Treaty convergence criteria, was 554.7 billion pesetas ($3.9 billion) in the four months to April. Figures for April on its own showed a surplus of 407.4 billion pesetas.
Despite the sharp improvement, analysts said it was unlikely Spain would undershoot its target to end 1997 with a central state deficit at 2.5 percent of GDP.

"You can't multiply by three this 0.7 percent and say they will likely end the year with a state budget deficit at 2.1 percent of GDP. In past years, the Spanish deficit was higher in the second and third quarters than in the first quarter," said Riccardo Barbieri, economist at Morgan Stanley in London.

Analysts also stressed that the "holy grail" of 3.0 percent deficit-to-GDP ratio to qualify for Europe's single currency refers not only to the central government but to the whole public administration.

But some analysts were not impressed by the figures because Spain's deficit, when measured on a cash basis, rose in the first four months by 30 percent to 454 billion pesetas versus the same period one year ago.

The central government's public deficit on a national account basis measures accrued revenues and expenditures for a given period, while the deficit on a cash basis registers actual money movements during a given month. Until January of this year, Spain only published data on a cash basis.
Even on a cash basis, the deficit through April narrowed versus March when the shortfall was running 37.1 percent higher versus the first quarter of 1996.
A healthy trend in revenues added to optimism, analysts said.
Total income rose 13.3 percent in the first four months to 5.99 trillion pesetas. Excluding 505 billion pesetas from privatisation proceeds, revenues rose 7.9 percent in the period.

"There is very strong growth in revenues. This is really encouraging because, given the fact the government is keeping expenditures under control, it now seems that the deficit goal is within reach," said Morgan Stanley's Barbieri.
From January to April, direct taxes rose 15.7 percent which compares in a favourable way to the 7.1 percent forecast in the budget law for all of 1997.
At the same time, the government brought forward some expenditures anticipated later in the year, for example interest payments.

"In the first quarter, we had an imbalance due to the fact that few expenditures had been brought forward," Budget Secretary of State Jose Folgado told a news conference. "We still have a slight imbalance."
"It's not easy to make a comparison. We have the cash deficit strictly influenced by differences in the payments calendar," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
